description.title: Ukrainian Children SOS
description.paragraph1: — is a charitable organization that provides comprehensive support to Ukrainian children affected by the war. The foundation's main goal is to give every child a sense of safety, care, and hope.
description.paragraph2: — cares for orphans, children with serious illnesses, children from orphanages, low-income families, and also provides assistance to children's homes, rehabilitation centers, and specialized schools.
description.paragraph3: The foundation implements humanitarian programs, organizes psychological and emotional support, recovery camps, educational initiatives, and direct fundraising for families in need.

directions.title: Our main areas of work
directions.children: We support children who have lost their parents, suffer from serious illnesses, or grow up in orphanages.
directions.families: We help families facing hardship and those raising seriously ill children.
directions.institutions: We support institutions that care for children — from orphanages to specialized schools and rehabilitation centers.

description.title: About the Foundation
description.p1: Ukrainian Children SOS is a charity that supports Ukrainian children whose childhoods have been shattered by war. We stand with those who lost parents, their homes, or lived through trauma. We help them not only survive, but believe in life again.
description.p2: Our mission is to give every child a sense of care, safety, and hope for a brighter future.
description.p3: We organize rehabilitation camps, provide psychological support, and deliver aid to families and institutions that care for children. Together with volunteers, professionals, and donors, we create spaces where children can laugh, learn, and dream again.
description.p4: Ukrainian Children SOS offers more than help — it gives children a future.

hero.subtitle1: Every initiative of Ukrainian Children SOS is real action.
hero.subtitle2: We create projects that bring children support, joy, new
hero.subtitle3: opportunities, and hope for a better future.

yarmarky.title: Charity Fairs
yarmarky.p1:
One of the warmest and most effective ways to support our children is through charity fairs and events.
These gatherings not only help raise essential funds but also become a space of unity for people who want to support children affected by the war.
yarmarky.p2: At the fairs, you can find handmade crafts, treats, books, clothes, and other items — especially touching are those created by the children themselves and volunteers. Every purchase is a small but meaningful contribution to a good cause.
yarmarky.p3: Charity events include concerts, auctions, sports events, and creative evenings. Taking part is not just a way to support the foundation — it's a chance to create change. All funds are directed to children's needs: housing, medicine, clothes, psychological care, and educational initiatives. And most importantly — these events give children emotional support, helping them feel cared for.
yarmarky.p4: We invite everyone to join our events. Together we can give children not only help but also faith in a brighter future.

children_heroes.title: Children of Heroes in London
children_heroes.p1:
"Children of Heroes" is a long-term project by Ukrainian Children SOS focused on providing psychological and emotional support to children who lost one or both parents because of the war.
The goal of the initiative is to create a safe space where children can feel care, restore their inner balance, and believe in the future again.
children_heroes.p2: As part of the project, we organize rehabilitation programs, creative camps, trips, and meetings, as well as individual assistance for those who need it most.
children_heroes.p3: The program includes psychological counseling, art therapy, joint activities with volunteers, and events that build trust and support. A special role is played by Ukrainian communities abroad, who warmly welcome these children and help them adapt to new environments.
children_heroes.p4: "Children of Heroes" is not only about help. It is about faith. About warmth that can be given even in the darkest times. It is a chance for every child to understand: they are not alone.

description.title: Stories of Ukrainian Children
description.p1: This section gathers the stories of children who have suffered as a result of the full-scale war: those who were wounded, killed, abducted, or illegally detained by Russian military or occupying authorities.
description.p2: You will also find materials about children who were able to return home after deportation to Russia or Belarus, or after being forcibly taken to temporarily occupied territories.

vlad.title: Vlad, 19 years old, Kherson
vlad.subtitle: forcibly transferred by Russians to a military college, returned to Ukraine in 2024
vlad.p1:
During the occupation of Kherson, Russian soldiers began searching for families with children who were not enrolled in local schools.
At first, Vlad's mother hid him and other children at home. One day, Russian soldiers with weapons entered the house when Vlad was alone. He was forced to pack his things and go with them — to an unknown destination and for an indefinite time.
vlad.p2: Vlad was moved between camps in Yevpatoria and Lazurne. There he was punished for protesting — such as removing the Russian flag — and was even held in isolation. Vlad witnessed how other children were humiliated, beaten, and forced to record apology videos.
vlad.p3: After the de-occupation of Kherson, his mother Tetiana filed a report about her son's disappearance and turned to the organization Save Ukraine. To reach the occupied territory, she had to travel through Poland, Belarus, and Russia. Before Vlad's return, she was detained, interrogated by FSB officers, and forced to spend the night in horrific conditions. Later, she learned that her plan may have been betrayed.
vlad.p4: Vlad and Tetiana were released only after they recorded a video praising Russia. Their documents and phones were returned, and after more than 12 hours of waiting at the border, they were finally allowed to leave.

illia.title: Illia, 11 years old, Mariupol
illia.subtitle: His childhood was destroyed by explosions, but he dreams of saving others
illia.p1: Illia is a child who has endured a lot of pain in his short life. When his hometown of Mariupol was recently shelled by Russians, his mother was killed, and Illia himself received multiple shrapnel wounds.
illia.p2: The occupiers took the boy to a hospital in Donetsk, where he suffered even more physical and emotional pain. The surgery was performed without anesthesia.
illia.p3:
"Now you must say not 'Glory to Ukraine,' but 'Glory to Ukraine as part of Russia,'" mocked the adults.
He was forced to write in Russian and was humiliated morally. Despite everything, the boy bravely endured every trial.
illia.p4: Thanks to his grandmother Olena, the government, and volunteer organizations, Illia was rescued from deportation. Now he is undergoing rehabilitation and dreams of becoming a doctor.

sasha.title: Sasha, 7 years old, Odesa
sasha.subtitle: Seven-year-old Sasha went through pain, amputation, and prosthetics — but returned to her beloved gymnastics.
sasha.p1: Seven-year-old Sasha is one of more than a thousand children who have suffered severe injuries as a result of the war unleashed by Russia against Ukraine. An enemy rocket struck the house where she lived with her parents.
sasha.p2: She was taken to a local hospital with multiple traumas. Doctors' predictions were dire — her lower leg had to be amputated.
sasha.p3:
Ahead lay seven months of painful recovery, two prosthetics, and countless tears.
But Sasha did not give up. She continues to do what she loves most — gymnastics.
sasha.p4: However, her mother admits that now her life is a constant struggle, one that remains hidden from the cameras and awards.

bohdan.title: Bohdan, 8 years old, Bakhmut
bohdan.subtitle: Bohdan was left an orphan after a rocket strike. He was scared, but he never stopped searching.
bohdan.p1:
His parents were killed by an enemy shell right on the street. At that time, Bohdan's mother was seven months pregnant. Bohdan was staying at a neighbor's, and when everyone fell asleep, he took his bike at night and rode to the site of the terrible event to see his parents.
His little heart refused to believe that his mom and dad were gone.
bohdan.p3: Law enforcement officers rescued Bohdan. They came for him, collected his things, evacuated him from the war zone, fed him, and tried to comfort him.
bohdan.p4: Now he is slowly returning to life — without his mom and dad, but with people around him who did not let him be completely alone.

margarita.title: Margarita, Mariupol
margarita.subtitle: Margo lost almost her entire family, but she keeps dreaming and wishing happiness for other children.
margarita.p1: Margo from Mariupol lost nearly all of her loved ones at once: her father, brother, two grandmothers, uncle, and godparents.
margarita.p2:
"I was in shock, but I didn't cry," she recalls.

Out of 12 people who were in the house during the shelling, only three survived.

"I talk to my dad through the window. He can hear me, right?"
margarita.p3:
Margarita went through rehabilitation, knows what helps her calm down, and speaks with psychologists like an adult.
She dreams of becoming a detective.
margarita.p35:
Sometimes she remembers the "Veselka" Park in Mariupol, where she always felt happy.
She warmly recalls how her grandmother taught her to read.
margarita.p4: Despite losing her hometown and family, Margo wishes Ukrainian children happiness and strength to keep living.
